analysis.one_liner: Strips professional baseball's century-old exemption from federal antitrust laws.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee in January 2023 and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Since a 1922 Supreme Court decision, baseball has been the only major professional sport exempt from federal antitrust laws, which are the rules that let governments and private parties challenge monopolies and unfair business practices. This bill would declare that professional baseball teams and leagues are fully subject to those laws, just like other businesses. That could open the door to legal challenges over franchise monopolies, ticket and TV pricing, and rules restricting players. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing, vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Baseball fans, who could see more competition — potentially more teams, lower ticket and TV prices, and challenges to exclusive territorial rights — and professional baseball players, who would gain the same legal protections against league-imposed restraints that players in other sports have.

how_it_helps.text: It makes baseball's business subject to the antitrust laws — the laws against monopolies and unfair competition — which currently do not apply to professional baseball.
The bill states Congress's finding that professional baseball is a business operating in interstate commerce, undercutting the legal basis for the exemption.
It applies the rules prospectively only, so conduct before enactment would not be challenged, limiting disruption to existing arrangements.

analysis.who_pays: Major League Baseball team owners and the league itself, which would lose the unique legal protection that lets it operate as a monopoly, control franchise locations, and limit player movement without facing competition challenges.
analysis.who_pays_short: MLB team owners and the league

drawbacks.text: Baseball has operated under its antitrust exemption for a century, and the exemption is woven into how the league is structured — its reserve rules, franchise territories, and minor-league system all rest on it. Removing it could throw those arrangements into legal uncertainty and years of litigation, which even some baseball fans and analysts who support more competition worry about.
The bill is narrow: it covers only baseball, not the other major sports, so it would not create uniform antitrust rules across professional sports.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — letting competition law apply to one of the last industries exempt from it — is real but modest: fans might see lower prices and more options, and players would gain legal recourse against restraints. The cost is genuine legal uncertainty for a league whose whole structure was built on the exemption, and the bill gave Congress no transition plan. It was also a symbolic gesture from a small group of three members with no movement toward a hearing, so neither the benefit nor the risk was ever seriously tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Jeff Duncan introduced the bill on January 9, 2023, joined by Representatives Biggs and Bishop of North Carolina.
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day, which was the only action ever taken on it.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote followed, and the bill died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major League Baseball and its team owners, who keep the antitrust exemption that shields their league structure and business practices from competition law.

for.name: Rep. Jeff Duncan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to subject professional baseball to the antitrust laws.

for.name: Reps. Andy Biggs and Dan Bishop
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, the only cosponsors it attracted.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over antitrust law
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only three Republican sponsors and no recorded opposition, so no partisan divide was ever tested — it simply never moved.

industries.industry: Major League Baseball (team owners and the league)
industries.note: Baseball has enjoyed a unique exemption from antitrust law for about a century, letting it operate as a controlled monopoly — one league, fixed franchise territories, and tightly restricted player movement. This bill would strip that protection, exposing ticket pricing, franchise control, and player restraints to normal competition law.

Players could gain the right to challenge league restraints on their movement and pay in court, something the antitrust exemption currently blocks. In practice, the players' union has historically accepted the exemption as part of its labor agreements, so the benefit is uncertain.
